description: Genome sequencing reads an organism's entire genetic material. Automated fluorescent-dye sequencers appeared from 1986, and computers assembled the overlapping reads. The first genome of a free-living organism, the bacterium Haemophilus influenzae, was published in 1995. The international Human Genome Project released a draft in 2001 and declared completion in 2003; a finished rice genome followed in 2005.

claims: Finished rice genome published in 2005 by an international project

uncertainty: The 2001 draft was released alongside a competing private effort (Celera); the 2003 'complete' human sequence still had gaps, closed only in 2022. Plant genome completion dates differ by source (rice: completed 2004, published 2005).

description: Gene editing changes a chosen DNA sequence inside living cells. Earlier tools needed a custom protein for each target. In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier's teams showed that Cas9, a bacterial antiviral enzyme, could be guided by designed RNA to cut a chosen site, earning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Rules for edited crops differ between countries.

claims: Genome editing modifies specific sites in DNA
Legal status of edited crops unclear in some jurisdictions
Regulation of CRISPR-edited crops differs between countries (US clearance 2016)

uncertainty: Priority is contested: Virginijus Siksnys's group reported similar Cas9 results in 2012, and patent disputes over use in human cells (Broad Institute, 2013 work) followed. CRISPR repeats were noticed in bacteria in 1987 and their immune role was established only in 2005-2007.

description: A catalytic converter passes engine exhaust over platinum-group metals on a honeycomb, speeding reactions that clean it. Fitted widely to new United States cars from the 1975 model year to meet Clean Air Act limits, early converters oxidised carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons. Lead poisons the catalyst, so unleaded petrol spread alongside. Later rhodium-bearing designs also reduce nitrogen oxides.
uncertainty: Exhaust catalysts were patented earlier (Eugene Houdry, 1950s) but not adopted until emission law required them; adoption dates differ by country (Japan and Europe later than or alongside the US), so 1975 marks the US mass fitting.

description: Carbon capture separates carbon dioxide from gas streams for use or storage. Usually an amine solution absorbs the carbon dioxide, releasing it when heated. Patented around 1930 to purify natural gas, it supplied Texas oil fields from the 1970s. Storage aimed at limiting climate change began at Norway's Sleipner field in 1996; capture remains small beside global emissions.
uncertainty: Whether capture can reach climate-relevant scale is unresolved (the node's 'scale speculative'); most captured CO2 historically went to enhanced oil recovery rather than permanent storage. The 1930 patent date (R. R. Bottoms) and the early-1970s Texas projects are standard histories not re-checked here.

description: DNA sequencing reads the order of the four bases along a DNA strand. Two methods appeared in 1977: Frederick Sanger's chain termination and Allan Maxam and Walter Gilbert's chemical cleavage. Both sorted labelled fragments by length on gels and read the order from ladders of bands. That year Sanger's group also published the first complete DNA genome, virus phiX174.
uncertainty: The node's range 1975-1977 covers Sanger's earlier 'plus and minus' method (1975), which was used for phiX174; the chain-termination method followed in 1977. RNA sequences had been read earlier (1960s), so 'first reading of genetic text' applies to DNA methods specifically.
